subject: paediatrics
title: Paediatric dehydration: assess, rehydrate orally first, recheck

steps.tx: **Dehydration** in children is graded by thirst, eyes, tears, skin pinch, urine output, alertness and perfusion, because weight-based guesses mislead. Most dehydrated children are rehydrated with **oral rehydration solution in small frequent amounts**, continuing breastfeeding and feeds as advised. Shock (cold peripheries, weak pulse, reduced consciousness) needs urgent intravenous resuscitation and senior help (NICE NG84; WHO guidance).
steps.say: Grade dehydration by eyes, tears, skin pinch, urine and alertness. Oral rehydration first; shock needs urgent intravenous care.

steps.tx: Vomiting is managed with small, frequent sips rather than large drinks, and anti-diarrhoeal drugs have no routine place in children. **Blood in stool, bile-stained vomiting, severe pain or a very young infant** changes the pathway and needs senior assessment. Reassess hydration after every rehydration phase; the plan changes with the child, not the clock alone.
steps.say: Small frequent sips beat large drinks. Blood, bile, severe pain or a young infant means senior assessment.

steps.tx: Parents are taught the volumes, the pace and the danger signs (fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes, unusual sleepiness, blood in stool) before discharge, with written advice. Exact millilitre-per-kilogramme calculations follow current NICE and WHO charts at the bedside and are flagged here rather than approximated.
steps.say: Teach parents volumes, pace and danger signs in writing. Exact calculations follow bedside charts, not approximation.
